title: Poland, 1939: five dates, different kinds of change
subtitle: An introduction to the first Ostfront Atlas timeline
author: R.G. Cruise
body:
Poland’s partition in 1939 poses a problem that a map of the final dividing line cannot resolve: how did military conquest acquire the institutions and language of a political settlement while the state being partitioned continued to reject it? On 30 September, Ambassador Jerzy Potocki formally informed Washington that his government regarded the German–Soviet agreement as illegal and intended to recover Poland’s territory. His protest supplies a useful point of departure. Effective possession, the occupiers’ asserted jurisdiction and international recognition developed along different paths, and understanding their relationship requires following the successive decisions through which the partition was imposed. [1] The five dates in this collection trace that process from August to October. They mark a diplomatic bargain, two invasions, a revised territorial agreement and the establishment of German civilian administration. Their sequence explains both the accumulation of coercive power and its limits: the invaders could occupy land, appoint officials and punish inhabitants without obtaining Polish acceptance of their authority. This introduction provides the conceptual and chronological framework; the dated chapters examine how those changes were negotiated, fought over and experienced. The country being invaded must first be understood on its own terms. Interwar Poland extended considerably farther east than Poland does today. The Treaty of Riga of 18 March 1921 had established the Polish–Soviet frontier that remained in place until 1939. The eastern borderlands contained communities with different languages, religions and political attachments; they cannot be represented adequately as a single population awaiting one national destiny. Their diversity would become a subject of German and Soviet bargaining and propaganda, but it did not give either neighbouring government the consent of the people over whom it claimed authority. [2] [3]

23 August: bargaining over other countries

The Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact changed the strategic conditions under which Germany could attack Poland. Its public provisions promised nonaggression between Germany and the Soviet Union, consultation and the avoidance of support for a third power fighting either signatory. Those promises mattered because they reduced the immediate danger that Hitler’s attack would bring Soviet opposition. Yet the published treaty was only one part of the transaction. The governments also negotiated a secret protocol dealing with territories whose inhabitants and representatives had no part in the agreement. [4] For Poland, the protocol described an approximate division of interests along the Narew, Vistula and San rivers, leaving open whether any independent Polish state would remain. Its wider provisions concerned the Baltic states, Finland and Bessarabia. This was a framework for disposing of other countries’ futures, rather than a record of territory already conquered. It neither placed Soviet soldiers inside Poland on 23 August nor established the final occupation boundary reached later in September. [5] A sphere of influence was therefore a claim upon the future, dependent on subsequent decisions and the force available to implement them. This is the first distinction to carry into the atlas. The August map records an understanding between governments, while the later maps record qualified interpretations of occupation and administration. The [study of the pact](/articles/molotov-ribbentrop-pact-1939-08-23) explains the negotiations that connected these possibilities, including the failed alternatives and the territorial inducements that brought Berlin and Moscow together.

1 September: military advantage meets resistance

Germany’s invasion turned diplomatic opportunity into an attempt to destroy the Polish armed forces. The geography favoured converging attacks: East Prussia supplied an approach from the north, German territory to the west supported the main offensive, and the southern approaches through Slovakia added another threat. Polish commanders faced a difficult choice between defending exposed industrial and population centres and withdrawing towards a shorter position that would surrender them. German strength in armour, aircraft and mobile formations made the problem more urgent, but the outcome still depended on fighting, communications, crossings and the movement of supplies. [6] German operational mobility made it possible to bypass positions and threaten communications beyond them, but a leading column’s progress did not measure the security of the country through which it had passed. The Bzura counteroffensive, beginning on 9 September, exposed that vulnerability. Kutrzeba’s forces struck the flank of the German Eighth Army and compelled a substantial response; the subsequent German concentration then threatened the attackers with encirclement. The episode explains how Polish forces could achieve a local reversal while their strategic position continued to deteriorate. The distinction between tactical action and the campaign as a whole is essential to assessing both Polish resistance and German advantage. [7] Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September, internationalising the conflict. Chamberlain’s announcement to Parliament explicitly connected British belligerency to Germany’s failure to promise an end to the aggression and withdrawal from Poland. A declaration, however, was different from military relief. The limited French advance in the Saar and the developing British deployment did not remove the immediate pressure on the Polish armies. Their allies were preparing for a prolonged conflict while Poland needed help within days. The [study of 1 September](/articles/german-invasion-poland-1939-09-01) follows that mismatch alongside the fighting and the violence inflicted on civilians. [8] [9] [10]

17 September: invasion from the east

The Red Army crossed Poland’s eastern frontier while Polish forces were still fighting Germany. Moscow presented its action as necessary protection for Ukrainians and Belarusians after an alleged collapse of the Polish state. The Soviet note reproduced in contemporary American diplomatic correspondence makes the reasoning explicit: it claimed that the disappearance of Polish government had released the Soviet Union from its treaty obligations and justified entry. That document is evidence of the excuse offered by the invading government. Its claims must be tested against the continued operation of Polish authorities, resistance in the field and recognition abroad. [11] For the people inside Poland, the second invasion transformed the meaning of the east. A direction of retreat from the German advance became another direction from which hostile forces approached. The Polish leadership crossed into Romania during the night of 17–18 September and was interned; troops sought routes towards Romania and Hungary, while other formations resisted Soviet attacks. Fighting at Grodno and elsewhere showed that the new occupation was imposed, even though the disparity of forces and the existing war against Germany sharply restricted Polish choices. [12] Britain’s response illustrates the restricted consequences that diplomatic opposition could have. In his report of 18 September, Ambassador Joseph Kennedy recorded Alexander Cadogan’s view that the Anglo-Polish agreement had not automatically placed Britain at war with the Soviet Union. The Polish ambassador had requested a formal protest, and British officials disputed Moscow’s claim that Poland’s government had disappeared. Recognition and protest thus continued alongside a refusal to enlarge the war. The [study of the Soviet invasion](/articles/soviet-invasion-poland-1939-09-17) follows the implications of that decision for Polish leaders, soldiers and civilians who confronted the second invading army. [13]

Diplomatic continuity

Recognition after territorial defeat

On 2 October 1939, U.S. Secretary of State Cordell Hull affirmed that Washington still regarded the Polish government as existing, despite the force used against the country. The FRUS editors preserve this statement in a note alongside the documents on occupation. Recognition sustained Poland’s standing in diplomatic relations even where its government could no longer exercise power on the ground. This small documentary detail makes the gap between conquest and political extinction unusually clear.

[14]

28 September: negotiating the division after invasion

The German–Soviet Boundary and Friendship Treaty revised the August bargain. Its public text declared the agreed boundary definitive and assigned administrative reorganisation on either side to the two signatories. The accompanying secret protocol transferred Lithuania into the Soviet sphere, subject to a territorial reservation, while assigning the Lublin province and part of the Warsaw province to Germany. The later partition therefore cannot be read as the straightforward implementation of an unchanged August line. The occupiers were adjusting their arrangement as the military and political situation developed. [15] [16] Warsaw capitulated on the same date, but its surrender and the treaty were separate events. [10] The city’s defenders were ending a siege; the governments in Moscow were asserting the authority to decide Poland’s territorial future. Polish forces continued fighting after Warsaw’s capitulation, and the final major campaign fighting at Kock ended in early October. There was no single moment at which every Polish formation surrendered, every occupation boundary became effective and every political question was settled. [17] The agreement also had an international purpose. In a joint declaration, Germany and the Soviet Union urged an end to the war between Germany and the Western powers and sought to place responsibility for its continuation on Britain and France. That argument treated the gains of conquest as an accomplished settlement before asking other governments to accept peace. The [study of 28 September](/articles/german-soviet-boundary-treaty-1939-09-28) examines the treaty’s public and secret provisions, economic arrangements, Polish rejection and the responses in London, Paris and Washington. [18]

26 October: making occupation a system of government

The October date concerns the institutions through which Germany governed the territory it controlled. Annexed western and northern districts were incorporated into the Reich, while the General Government under Hans Frank administered another portion of occupied Poland. The latter initially comprised the districts of Kraków, Warsaw, Radom and Lublin. It was an imposed German administration, not a surviving Polish government. The distinction between annexation and the General Government reflected different territorial arrangements within the same project of domination. [19] The interval between a decree and its implementation helps explain how this new authority was constructed. The founding decree for the General Government bore the date 12 October, whereas civilian administration took effect on 26 October; annexation proceeded through its own decrees and effective dates. Appointments, jurisdictions and administrative boundaries required further decisions after the territorial bargain. The [study of 26 October](/articles/german-occupation-administration-1939-10-26) traces that institutional process into labour, education, property and the regulation of daily life, where changes in authority became concrete obligations for the population. [20] Soviet occupation followed a different administrative sequence. Controlled elections in October supplied assemblies that requested incorporation into the Soviet Union, followed by formal incorporation measures on **1–2 November**. Those acts should not be dated to the invasion itself or treated as freely expressed popular consent. The German and Soviet systems differed in institutions, ideology and procedure; both used the power acquired through invasion to override Poland’s territorial independence. Their distinct chronologies are essential to understanding the different claims shown on the maps. [21]

The people inside the partition—and the Poland that continued

For civilians, the sequence was experienced through displacement, violence and changing demands. Jewish families fleeing the German advance often travelled east, only to encounter a second occupation and increasingly dangerous crossings. Some later attempted to return because separation from relatives, lack of money and uncertainty about shelter could make remaining away from home unbearable. Such decisions cannot be judged as though refugees possessed a reliable forecast of everything that would follow. The records of flight show people choosing among immediate dangers with incomplete information. [22] Social experience also resists an explanation organised solely by nationality. Stanisław Boridczenko’s research examines the interaction of national, class and local attachments in responses to the arriving armies. The value of that approach lies in its attention to the circumstances in which people acted: political expectations, remembered grievances and immediate danger could pull in different directions. This variety must be reconstructed from evidence about particular communities and witnesses. It cannot be inferred from the invaders’ claim to represent an entire people. [3] Persecution was already acquiring an administrative form. Heydrich’s instructions of 21 September linked the concentration of Jewish populations to railway access and required Jewish councils to carry out German demands under threat. Census-taking, movement and economic decisions became instruments of coercion. This early process must be understood in its own chronology: it was part of the developing occupation, without being identical to the later, fully developed machinery of extermination. The October study follows how political and racial objectives were translated into offices, regulations and acts of dispossession. [23] Polish political life also continued beyond the occupied territory. Władysław Raczkiewicz became president and Władysław Sikorski prime minister in France on 30 September. The United States explicitly affirmed continued recognition of the Polish government on 2 October. Within occupied Poland, underground organisation began to preserve a capacity for resistance. None of this restored the government’s ability to protect its population immediately. It did, however, prevent the occupiers’ description of Poland as an extinguished state from becoming an uncontested account of what had happened. [24] [14] [25]

Reading the maps and the studies together

The atlas separates events that a single end-of-campaign map would compress. Its dated views distinguish political boundaries, territorial control, administrative arrangements and military movement. An arrow indicates a direction or an explicitly identified operational objective; its tip should not automatically be read as the furthest position securely occupied on that day. A shaded area describes the kind of control identified in its legend and notes. Neither device confers legitimacy on the authority it represents. The survival of the prewar Polish outline makes it possible to compare those imposed changes against the territory over which they operated. The maps’ precision varies with their evidence. An agreement may specify a diplomatic division more clearly than reports establish when a village or crossing came under effective control. Regional shading and movement arrows should therefore be read with their dates, legends and qualifications. The studies make the same distinction in their citations: a treaty establishes its signatories’ commitments; a diplomatic report preserves the author’s information and judgments; an operational account has its own geographical and temporal limits. The linked references allow readers to move between the argument and the evidence on which it rests. Taken in sequence, the studies explain how an agreement concerning Poland became armed invasion, territorial renegotiation and an apparatus of rule. The outcome was a profound destruction of the government’s capacity to protect its inhabitants, accompanied by continuing resistance and diplomatic claims to independence. That combination gives the collection its central question: how far could the occupiers convert force into durable authority, and what forms of Polish political and social life survived the attempt? The chapters that follow address it through the decisions and experiences particular to each date.

summary: Five dates explain how diplomatic bargaining became invasion, partition and occupation—and why military defeat did not extinguish the Polish state.
sourceMethod: This introduction combines German–Soviet treaty texts, contemporary diplomatic correspondence, British parliamentary records, Polish documentary scholarship, military history and research on civilian experience. The main evidence includes the Institute for Western Affairs, the Polish Army Museum, the Institute of National Remembrance, The Historical Journal and the published Foreign Relations of the United States documents. Museum accounts supplement these sources. Official claims are attributed to their authors; military control, claimed annexation and diplomatic recognition are distinguished. The detailed studies supply the fuller operational and local evidence. Numbered superscripts link to sources below, and each source has a link back to its first citation.
